body:
What are the Major Rock Edicts?

The Major Rock Edicts are an important group of Ashoka's proclamations engraved on natural rock surfaces. The standard series contains 14 numbered edicts, although the surviving texts and their arrangement differ between locations.

The numbers are useful because several edicts are identified in objective examinations by their subject matter. For example, the edict dealing with medical treatment is different from the edict explaining religious tolerance or the one describing the conquest of Kalinga.

Major Rock Edicts 1–14

EdictPrincipal subject
1Restraint on animal slaughter and sacrifice; reduction of animals killed in the royal kitchen.
2Medical treatment for humans and animals; medicinal plants, wells and roadside trees.
3Respect for parents and others; generosity and restraint; official tours every 5 years.
4Promotion of dhamma contrasted with the earlier emphasis on warfare and harmful conduct.
5Appointment and duties of dhamma-mahamattas; concern for different groups and prisoners.
6Prompt attention to public affairs and arrangements for reports to reach the king at any time.
7Coexistence of different religious traditions and the value of self-control.
8Dhamma-yatras, or tours devoted to moral and religious purposes, instead of pleasure hunting.
9Greater value of ethical conduct than ceremonies performed merely for good fortune.
10Limited value of personal fame and glory unless they promote dhamma.
11Dhamma-dana, the gift of dhamma, and its moral value.
12Respect for other religious traditions, restraint in speech and avoidance of needless criticism.
13Kalinga conquest, reported deaths and deportations, remorse and dhamma-vijaya.
14Variations in the length, content and arrangement of inscriptions at different places.

Important distinctions between the edicts

Animal welfare and medical welfare are different subjects

Rock Edict 1 primarily addresses the killing of animals, whereas Rock Edict 2 concerns medical treatment and facilities benefiting people and animals. A question mentioning hospitals or medicinal plants therefore points to a different edict from a question about slaughter in the royal kitchen.

Officials and public reporting are different subjects

Rock Edict 5 deals with dhamma-mahamattas, appointed in the 13th year after coronation. Rock Edict 6 deals with prompt government business and the reporting of people's affairs to the emperor.

Religious coexistence and religious speech are different subjects

Rock Edict 7 expresses the wish that religious communities should coexist. Rock Edict 12 gives more specific guidance against praising one's own religion by disparaging others.

The Kalinga war and dhamma-vijaya belong to Edict 13

Edict 13 is especially important because it records the conquest in the 8th year after coronation, the reported losses and Ashoka's preference for conquest through dhamma.

Why the inscriptions are not identical everywhere

Major Rock Edict 14 itself explains that the messages were issued in different lengths and that every text did not necessarily appear at every location. Consequently, the standard count of 14 is a classification of the principal series, not a claim that all 14 survive on every inscribed rock.

The separate Kalinga Rock Edicts

At Dhauli and Jaugada in present-day Odisha, the standard Major Rock Edicts 11, 12 and 13 are absent from the local sequence. Instead, these sites contain 2 Separate Kalinga Rock Edicts, which give instructions relevant to administration in the conquered region.

The Separate Kalinga Edicts emphasise fair treatment by officials and the prevention of unjust imprisonment or harsh punishment. One expresses the emperor's paternal concern for the population through the statement that all people are his children.

The edict that describes Ashoka's remorse over Kalinga is Major Rock Edict 13, but that particular text is not found in the regular sequence at Dhauli and Jaugada. These Odisha sites preserve separate instructions associated with Kalinga instead.

Prelims focus

  • The standard Major Rock Edict series contains 14 edicts.
  • Rock Edict 2 concerns medical treatment for humans and animals.
  • Rock Edict 5 concerns dhamma-mahamattas.
  • Rock Edict 12 concerns religious tolerance and restraint in speech.
  • Rock Edict 13 records the Kalinga conquest and dhamma-vijaya.
  • Trap: Dhauli and Jaugada contain Separate Kalinga Edicts rather than the complete standard sequence of 14 Major Rock Edicts.

[Sources: S. Dhammika, The Edicts of King Asoka, The Fourteen Rock Edicts, 1–14, and The Kalinga Rock Edicts, 1–2, consulted 18 November 2026; NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6, Chapter 8, printed pp. 79–81; NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Chapter 2, printed pp. 32–34 and 48.]

title: The 14 Major Rock Edicts and Their Main Messages

body:
Rock inscriptions and pillar inscriptions

Ashoka's messages were engraved on different stone surfaces. A rock edict was inscribed on a natural rock or boulder. A pillar edict was engraved on a specially erected stone pillar.

Both forms could carry messages about dhamma and government. The distinction concerns the surface and the group of inscriptions, not a rule that rocks contained only moral teachings while pillars contained only administrative orders.

Mauryan pillars were often carefully polished and could carry sculpted animal capitals. The famous Lion Capital of Sarnath is associated with Ashoka and later became the basis of India's State Emblem. However, the artistic capital and the inscribed edict should be identified as different features of a pillar.

The 7 Major Pillar Edicts

The standard Major Pillar Edict series contains 7 numbered edicts. These principally address moral conduct and the ruler's duties.

Pillar edictPrincipal message
1Promotion of dhamma and the importance of sincere moral effort.
2Definition of dhamma through kindness, generosity, truthfulness and purity.
3Self-examination and avoidance of cruelty, anger, pride and jealousy.
4Duties of Rajjukas in administration and justice; a 3-day stay for prisoners sentenced to death.
5Protection of specified animals and restrictions on killing at certain times.
6Welfare of subjects and honouring different religious traditions.
7Summary of dhamma measures, public welfare works and the value of persuasion.

The expression 7 Major Pillar Edicts refers to 7 numbered proclamations. It does not mean that Ashoka erected only 7 pillars or that every surviving pillar carries the complete series.

Minor Rock Edicts

Minor Rock Edicts are shorter inscriptions that often reveal more specific aspects of Ashoka's religious commitments or instructions.

Some contain evidence of Ashoka's personal commitment to Buddhism. The inscription associated with Maski in Karnataka is particularly important because the king's personal name, Ashoka, appears there. Another important identification occurs at Gujarra in Madhya Pradesh.

The Bhabru or Bairat Edict, associated with Rajasthan, addresses the Buddhist Sangha and recommends particular Buddhist teachings. It must be distinguished from the general rock edicts intended for a wider population.

Minor Pillar Edicts and specific places

Some pillar inscriptions concern particular religious sites or institutions rather than the general series of 7 Major Pillar Edicts.

  • Rummindei or Lumbini, Nepal: An inscription records Ashoka's visit to the birthplace of the Buddha in the 20th year after coronation and a tax privilege for the village. The inscription states that the village was required to pay only one-eighth of its produce.
  • Nigalisagar, Nepal: An inscription concerns the stupa of the Buddha Kanakamuni.
  • Sarnath, Uttar Pradesh, and Sanchi, Madhya Pradesh: Minor pillar inscriptions include instructions concerning divisions within the Buddhist Sangha.

These inscriptions illustrate why an objective question must distinguish a Major Pillar Edict from a Minor Pillar Edict, even when both appear on pillars associated with Ashoka.

Why different kinds of inscriptions were issued

The variety of inscriptions reflects the range of Ashoka's concerns. Some conveyed general ethical duties, some instructed officials, some addressed the Buddhist community, and others recorded visits or privileges associated with particular places.

Their language and wording also varied by region. It is therefore important to identify an inscription by its type, subject and location, rather than treating all Ashokan inscriptions as identical.

Prelims focus

  • The standard Major Pillar Edict series contains 7 edicts.
  • Major Pillar Edict 2 explains qualities included in dhamma.
  • Major Pillar Edict 4 provides a 3-day stay for prisoners sentenced to death.
  • Maski in Karnataka is associated with the personal name Ashoka in an inscription.
  • Rummindei or Lumbini is associated with the Buddha's birthplace and a village tax privilege.
  • Trap: Major and Minor Pillar Edicts are different inscription groups; 7 Major Pillar Edicts does not mean 7 pillars.

[Sources: NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Chapter 2, printed pp. 32–33 and 47; NCERT, An Introduction to Indian Art, Part I, Class 11, Chapter 3, Arts of the Mauryan Period, printed pp. 19–20; S. Dhammika, The Edicts of King Asoka, Minor Rock Edicts, The Seven Pillar Edicts and The Minor Pillar Edicts, consulted 18 November 2026; UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Serial Nomination for Ashokan Edict Sites along the Mauryan Routes, location inventory submitted 11 February 2025, consulted 18 November 2026.]

title: Pillar Edicts, Minor Inscriptions and the Messages They Preserve

body:
Why the locations matter

Ashokan inscriptions have been found across a wide region extending beyond the boundaries of present-day India. Their distribution helps identify the places to which the emperor's messages were directed.

In objective examinations, a site may be paired with its present-day state or country, the type of inscription found there, or the script used. These are separate attributes: knowing that a place has an Ashokan inscription does not by itself identify whether the inscription is major, minor, on a rock or on a pillar.

Girnar: the important Gujarat connection

One of the principal Ashokan inscription sites is Girnar near Junagadh in Gujarat. The inscriptions are engraved on a large rock near the route towards the Girnar hills.

The Girnar site preserves the 14 Major Rock Edicts of Ashoka. They are written in a form of Prakrit using the Brahmi script.

The site is important because it shows that Ashoka's public instructions were communicated in the western part of the subcontinent as well as near the imperial capital. Its inscriptions address the same broad subjects found in the Major Rock Edict series, including ethical conduct, welfare and religious relations.

The Girnar rock is also associated with later inscriptions of other rulers, including Rudradaman and Skandagupta. These later texts are not Ashokan edicts merely because they occur at the same historical site.

Girnar = Junagadh = Gujarat = Major Rock Edicts. The Ashokan inscriptions are associated with Prakrit language and Brahmi script.

Important inscription sites and present-day locations

SitePresent-day location and significance
GirnarJunagadh, Gujarat; Major Rock Edicts.
KalsiUttarakhand; Major Rock Edicts.
DhauliOdisha; rock edicts including Separate Kalinga Edicts.
JaugadaOdisha; rock edicts including Separate Kalinga Edicts.
ErragudiAndhra Pradesh; Major Rock Edicts and Minor Rock Edicts.
SannatiKarnataka; Ashokan rock-edict inscriptions.
SoparaMaharashtra; fragments of Major Rock Edicts.
MaskiKarnataka; Minor Rock Edict using the name Ashoka.
GujarraMadhya Pradesh; Minor Rock Edict using the name Ashoka.
BairatRajasthan; associated with Minor Rock Edicts.
SarnathUttar Pradesh; pillar inscription and famous Lion Capital.
SanchiMadhya Pradesh; Minor Pillar Edict associated with the Buddhist Sangha.
LumbiniNepal; Minor Pillar Edict recording the Buddha's birthplace.
Mansehra and ShahbazgarhiPresent-day Pakistan; Major Rock Edicts in Kharosthi script.
KandaharAfghanistan; Ashokan inscriptions including Greek and Aramaic.

Language and script: 2 different facts

A language is the system of words and expressions used to communicate meaning. A script is the system of written signs used to represent a language. One must therefore distinguish what language an inscription contains from the script in which that language is written.

Most Ashokan inscriptions in the Indian subcontinent use Prakrit language and Brahmi script. In parts of the northwest, Prakrit inscriptions were written in Kharosthi. In Afghanistan, inscriptions also occur in Greek and Aramaic.

This variation helped make the emperor's messages accessible to different regional audiences. It also means that the statement all Ashokan inscriptions were written in Brahmi is incorrect.

A common confusion involving Gujarat

The name Gujarra can be mistaken for Gujarat. However, Gujjara is an inscription site in Madhya Pradesh. The major Ashokan inscription site in Gujarat is Girnar near Junagadh.

Similarly, Dhauli and Jaugada are both in Odisha, while Kalsi is in Uttarakhand. Correctly matching these names with their locations is more useful than merely memorising that all are Ashokan sites.

Prelims focus

  • Girnar near Junagadh, Gujarat, contains Ashoka's 14 Major Rock Edicts.
  • Dhauli and Jaugada are in Odisha; Kalsi is in Uttarakhand.
  • Maski is in Karnataka; Gujjara is in Madhya Pradesh.
  • Most inscriptions use Prakrit language and Brahmi script.
  • Mansehra and Shahbazgarhi are associated with Kharosthi script.
  • Trap: Gujjara in Madhya Pradesh is not the same as Girnar in Gujarat.

[Sources: NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Chapter 2, map and discussion of Ashokan inscriptions, printed pp. 32–33 and 46–47; NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6, Chapter 8, printed pp. 79–81; District Administration, Junagadh, Government of Gujarat, Ashok Shilalekh, site description, consulted 18 November 2026; Archaeological Survey of India, Dehradun Circle, Kalsi monument description, consulted 18 November 2026; UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Serial Nomination for Ashokan Edict Sites along the Mauryan Routes, site inventory submitted 11 February 2025, consulted 18 November 2026.]
title: Locations of Ashokan Edicts: Girnar, Kalinga and Other Major Sites
